title: Water Rights During the Long Dry
scenario: Water master Tomás Villalobos in Spain's Murcia region must allocate a diminished reservoir release this summer. Irrigators with century-old rights want their full share for orchards that employ thousands, the city of 200,000 needs drinking water priority, and a wetland downstream that shelters rare birds will dry out without a minimum flow. The law is ambiguous on priority in this kind of shortfall, and the regional government has left the call to him.
options: Guarantee full city supply first, then irrigators by seniority, leaving the wetland with whatever remains.
Reserve a minimum flow for the wetland and share the remaining water proportionally between the city and the irrigators.
Prioritise irrigators' historic rights and the jobs they support, asking the city to ration and the wetland to wait.

title: Overfished Cod and the Quota Lottery
scenario: Fisheries council member Bjarni Thorsteinsson in Iceland has to divide a sharply reduced cod quota. Large trawler companies argue that their capital investments and efficient operations justify bigger shares, while small coastal boat owners say that tradition and rural survival do. Scientists want an even deeper cut than the one proposed. Whatever the council decides will shape which villages survive and how quickly the stock recovers.
options: Allocate by historic catch share, rewarding past investment and efficiency and favouring the larger firms.
Allocate a protected portion to small coastal boats first, supporting villages even if overall efficiency drops.
Cut the quota further as scientists advise and share the pain equally, accepting greater hardship in the short run.

title: Grazing Commons Without Fences
scenario: Elder Nomvula Dlamini chairs a village grazing committee in KwaZulu-Natal where the common pasture is degrading as herds grow. A few wealthy households own large herds, while many poor families have two or three cows. Setting a per-household cap would hit the rich more and help the pasture, but a per-animal fee would raise funds for fencing and water. The wealthy hold political influence in the chiefdom, and any rule needs broad consent.
options: Impose an equal cap per household, which limits the largest herds and distributes access evenly.
Introduce a per-animal fee funding rangeland repair, allowing the wealthy to keep large herds if they pay.
Delay any rule for a season while the committee surveys herd sizes, accepting more degradation to build consensus.

title: Groundwater Tax for the Almond Belt
scenario: State water board chair Harpreet Gill in Punjab, India, is weighing a metered tax on groundwater pumped for rice. The aquifer is dropping by a metre each year, and some wells have already run dry for smaller farmers who cannot dig deeper. Larger farmers say a tax threatens food security and the state's role as the country's granary. A tax would raise money for drip irrigation grants but the grants might mostly benefit richer farmers first.
options: Introduce the groundwater tax immediately, protecting the aquifer and funding efficiency measures.
Delay the tax and expand subsidised drip irrigation first, hoping voluntary savings will slow depletion.
Introduce the tax with an exemption for small farmers, shifting the burden on larger farms and risking political backlash.
tension: equity between large and small farmers

title: A Fishing Quota for Newcomers
scenario: Community fisheries officer Moana Tuhiwai in the Cook Islands manages a lagoon with limited giant clam stocks. Young islanders returning from overseas want access to harvest, but older fishers fear overuse and want to preserve their share. Customary rules give priority to families with traditional rights, but the families concerned are dwindling and some have left. Moana must propose a rule to the elders at next week's meeting.
options: Restrict harvesting to families with traditional rights, preserving custom and stock but excluding the returnees.
Open the harvest to all residents under a shared quota, widening access at the risk of faster depletion.
Allow limited newcomer permits tied to community service and stock monitoring, a compromise that adds complexity.

title: Rationing Electricity in the Heat
scenario: Grid operator Dimitri Volkov in Kazakhstan must cut power to part of the network during a record cold snap as supply falls short. He can black out an industrial zone, risking job losses and equipment damage, rotate outages through residential neighbourhoods including one with a hospital annexe, or draw down hydropower reserves that farmers need for irrigation next summer. The decision is needed within the hour.
options: Cut the industrial zone first, protecting homes and clinics at the cost of economic loss.
Rotate outages through residential areas fairly while sparing hospitals, sharing the burden among households.
Draw down the reserves, keeping lights on now at the risk of water shortages for farmers next summer.

title: Seed Saving and the Patent Notice
scenario: Farmers' union lawyer Esperanza Quintero in Colombia is approached by smallholders who received a notice from a seed company claiming that saving seeds from its patented maize violates its rights. The seeds produce higher yields, but saving them was a long-standing practice that reduces costs. Fighting the case would be expensive and could end in precedent either way. The farmers' livelihoods and the region's seed diversity are at stake, and Esperanza has to advise them.
options: Advise fighting the case in court, defending traditional seed saving and seeking a precedent that protects farmers.
Advise a settlement with licensing terms, securing immediate relief and avoiding the risk of a damaging precedent.
Advise returning to local varieties for most plots, giving up the higher yields but avoiding legal exposure.

title: Rare Earth Tailings and the Orphaned Lake
scenario: Regional environment official Dr. Li Wenjun in Inner Mongolia must decide whether to extend an operating licence for a mine producing rare earths vital to wind turbines and electronics. The tailings lake leaks slowly, and nearby villagers' wells show rising contamination. The mine employs 6,000 people and supplies a national industry. Cleaning up would require closing part of the site for years. Her signature on the licence is the last step.
options: Extend the licence with a strict cleanup schedule, keeping jobs and supply while demanding remediation.
Suspend part of the operation until the leak is sealed, protecting villagers and accepting lost output and jobs.
Refuse to extend and require full closure and remediation, prioritising the villagers' health over industrial supply.
tension: industrial supply and jobs vs. villagers' health

title: The Last Shared Well
scenario: Imam and village councillor Yusuf Abdi in Somaliland oversees the last perennial well in a drought-stricken district. Pastoralist clans take turns watering their herds, but a newly arrived group of displaced families also needs water for their goats and for drinking. The well can supply roughly what the existing clans need, and any extra use will cause it to run dry earlier in the season. Tensions are rising as the displaced families wait.
options: Maintain the existing clan rotation, preserving local order and sustainable use but leaving the newcomers with limited access.
Allow newcomers drinking water only, not herd watering, balancing survival needs against the well's capacity.
Open the well fully to all, accepting that it may run dry sooner, rather than deny anyone water.

title: Allotment Gardens for Housing
scenario: City councillor Rebecca Ndiaye in Dublin faces a vote on rezoning a historic allotment site for 300 affordable homes. A housing waiting list of 9,000 families is growing, and the site is among the few city-owned plots available. The allotments feed around 150 households, host a bee-friendly meadow and have been tended for ninety years. The housing alternative sites would take years to prepare. She holds the deciding vote.
options: Vote to rezone for housing, giving priority to families in urgent need of homes.
Vote to retain the allotments, protecting a shared green space and food source and seeking other sites for housing.
Vote to rezone half of the site, building fewer homes and shrinking the gardens, with disappointment on both sides.
tension: housing need vs. shared green space

title: Fire Season Water Bombers
scenario: Regional fire chief Elena Marquez in Portugal has one water-bombing aircraft available during a wave of wildfires. One fire threatens a village of 800 people with only one escape road, another is burning through a protected cork oak forest that supports hundreds of rural livelihoods and rare lynx habitat. Both could be saved only partly. Winds are shifting, and she must send the aircraft in minutes.
options: Send the aircraft to the village, protecting human lives and homes and accepting loss of the forest.
Send the aircraft to the forest fire, trusting that the village can evacuate in time and protecting the shared ecosystem.
Hold the aircraft briefly to gather wind data before choosing, risking delay at a critical moment.
tension: human safety vs. ecosystem and livelihoods

title: Selling the Village Spring
scenario: Cooperative chair Mariam Sesay in Sierra Leone is offered a sum by a bottled water company for exclusive rights to a spring that serves four villages. The payment would fund a school and clinic, and the company promises piped water to the nearest village. But the company's extraction could reduce spring flow in the dry season, and future leadership would be bound by a thirty-year agreement. The villages are divided on the offer.
options: Accept the offer, using the funds and promised piping to improve education, health and access to water today.
Reject the offer, keeping control of the spring and its management by future generations in the villages.
Negotiate a smaller extraction limit and a shorter term, risking the company walking away from the deal.

title: Rationing the Last Antibiotics
scenario: Hospital pharmacist Dr. Suriya Chandran in Sri Lanka faces a shortage of a last-resort antibiotic that treats resistant infections. Using it on every severe case speeds up bacterial resistance, rendering it useless for future patients, but withholding it from some current patients could be fatal. A critical-care consultant wants broad access, while the infection control team asks for strict limits. A board meeting decides the hospital policy tomorrow.
options: Adopt broad access for all severe cases, prioritising the lives at risk right now.
Adopt strict criteria limiting use to cases with confirmed resistance, preserving effectiveness for future patients.
Allow broad access for a trial period while closely monitoring resistance data, deferring a final policy.

title: Rooftop Solar on Shared Blocks
scenario: Housing cooperative treasurer Ahmed Benali in Algiers must decide how to share a limited number of solar panels on an apartment building's roof. Residents on the top floors have the most roof access and vote for the panels to power their own flats. Those on lower floors say the roof is a shared asset and want a rotating supply or shared pool. Some residents cannot afford even the small connection fee. The cooperative meets Saturday.
options: Assign panels to top-floor flats, reflecting where the equipment sits and keeping administration simple.
Pool the output equally among all households, treating the roof as shared and subsidising those who cannot pay.
Allocate by income need first, then equal share, privileging the poorest households but triggering resentment.

title: The Shared Lake Treaty
scenario: Diplomat Dr. Alisher Karimov in Central Asia is negotiating the share of a transboundary river between an upstream country that wants to run hydropower dams in winter and a downstream country whose farms need water in summer. The upstream country is poorer and needs electricity for heating in winter, while the downstream country's farmers face drought. Both sides are inflexible. He must propose a framework for the final session.
options: Propose a winter-power priority with compensation to the downstream country, supporting upstream heating needs.
Propose a summer-water priority for downstream farmers with energy compensation upstream, protecting food production.
Propose a flexible seasonal rule triggered by hydrological conditions, an approach that is complex and hard to enforce.

title: Dividing the Salmon Run
scenario: Tribal fisheries manager Daniel Redcloud in Washington State has a treaty right to half the salmon run, but the run has collapsed to a fraction of its historic size. If his tribe takes its full share, the spawning population may not be sustained. Sport fishers and commercial boats have already agreed to deep cuts, and some resent that the tribe has not. Taking less honours conservation but could be read as a loss of treaty rights.
options: Harvest the full treaty share, protecting a right that was hard won and may not be restored later.
Take a reduced share voluntarily this year, leading by example to protect the run while formally reserving the right.
Seek a joint agreement with all parties to share cuts proportionally under binding enforcement, taking longer to negotiate.
tension: fairness to other users vs. justice for past wrongs

title: Electric Buses or More Bus Routes
scenario: Transport director Funmilayo Adebayo in Ibadan has funding for either fifty electric buses on existing routes or two hundred diesel buses extending service to underserved suburbs. The electric buses would cut local air pollution and emissions and lower running costs in the long term. The diesel buses would give hundreds of thousands of poorer residents access to jobs and clinics now. The funder requires a choice by the end of the financial year.
options: Buy the electric buses, investing in cleaner air and lower costs over the long term.
Buy the diesel buses, expanding access for those who currently have no service.
Buy a mix of about thirty electric and sixty diesel buses, reaching fewer people and polluting less than either extreme.
tension: environmental quality vs. access to opportunity

title: A Common Orchard and the Late Frost
scenario: Neighbourhood association head Svetlana Petrova in Bulgaria manages a community orchard where all residents may pick fruit. A late frost has left only a fraction of the usual crop, and some residents have begun picking early and taking large amounts to sell at markets. Others, including elderly households that rely on the fruit, are left with little. Svetlana can set picking limits, restrict access to registered households, or do nothing and let the community sort it out.
options: Set a strict per-household picking limit, enforced by volunteers, to share the small harvest evenly.
Restrict picking to registered households who rely on the orchard, excluding market sellers and outside visitors.
Take no action and let neighbours settle it themselves, preserving informality at the risk of conflict and unfair outcomes.

title: Community Forest Timber Quota
scenario: Forest user group chair Bimala Gurung in Nepal leads a community forest that has regrown over thirty years and now holds valuable timber. Households want to harvest a large portion to repair earthquake-damaged houses and pay school fees. Foresters recommend a much smaller sustainable harvest to protect the forest's recovery and the water source below. Not all households are equally affected by the damage. Bimala must propose a harvest plan to the assembly.
options: Propose a large harvest, meeting the urgent housing and education needs of households now.
Propose the smaller sustainable harvest, protecting the forest and the water supply for the long term.
Propose a medium harvest prioritised for the most damaged households, leaving others to wait for a later round.
tension: equal share vs. priority by hardship

title: Wi-Fi Towers and Sacred Hills
scenario: Telecom engineer Pita Kawharu in New Zealand has to decide the site for a tower that would bring emergency mobile coverage to a remote valley. The best location sits on a hill that local Maori consider sacred, while alternative sites would give weaker coverage, leaving some farms and a hiker route without signal. A recent search-and-rescue incident underscores the coverage gap. Consultation with the tribal council has been inconclusive.
options: Build on the sacred hill for the best coverage, giving priority to safety in emergencies.
Build on the weaker alternative site, honouring the sacred status and accepting coverage gaps.
Postpone construction until consultation reaches a consensus, accepting that the coverage gap remains for months.

title: Public Beach, Private Dunes
scenario: Coastal manager Lorenzo Bianchi in Italy oversees an eroding beach where a private resort wants to build a sea wall that will protect its hotel and the village behind it. But the wall would accelerate erosion on the neighbouring public beach, where local families, fishers and a turtle nesting site depend on the sand. The resort offers to fund sand replenishment, though only for a few years. The permit decision is his.
options: Approve the wall with the resort-funded replenishment, protecting jobs and the village while accepting risks to the public beach.
Deny the permit, protecting the public beach and turtles and leaving the hotel to adapt or relocate.
Approve a softer design with dune planting and a sunset clause, a less effective protection that all sides may resent.

title: Vaccine Cold Chain or Fishing Ice
scenario: Regional health officer Dr. Pele Tuilagi in Samoa has a single solar-powered freezer unit funded by a donor, and two villages are competing for it. One village wants it for vaccine storage for its clinic, which currently relies on a two-hour boat trip. The other wants it to store fish and build a small fishing cooperative that could lift incomes. Donor conditions permit either use but not both. The boat leaves in the morning.
options: Place the freezer at the clinic to improve vaccine access and child health.
Place the freezer at the fishing cooperative to build local income that can fund health later.
Place the freezer at the clinic but share a small portion of its capacity with the cooperative, risking spoilage of vaccines.

title: Compost Rights in the Slum Market
scenario: Waste cooperative leader Rosa Mamani in La Paz, Bolivia, collects organic waste from a market and sells compost to farmers. A private firm now proposes taking over waste collection for the whole market under a city contract, promising modern trucks and lower costs. The city welcomes it, but the cooperative's forty informal workers would lose their access to the market's waste and their income. Rosa must decide whether to negotiate, resist, or join.
options: Negotiate to merge the cooperative into the firm's operation, accepting lower pay but keeping jobs for some workers.
Resist the contract publicly, defending the workers' access to the waste stream despite the city's preference.
Withdraw from the market and seek new sources of waste elsewhere, avoiding conflict but abandoning existing customers.

title: Allocating the Last Carbon Allowances
scenario: Cap-and-trade administrator Kenji Okamoto in Japan has to distribute a limited batch of free carbon allowances. A steel mill employing 3,000 in a depressed region says it needs them to stay competitive against imports. A hospital network and a public rail operator also apply, citing public service duties, and a start-up making low-carbon cement wants allowances to scale. Handing them all to one applicant means others pay higher costs. The deadline for allocations is Monday.
options: Allocate to the steel mill to protect jobs and regional stability.
Allocate to the hospital network and rail operator, prioritising essential public services.
Allocate to the low-carbon cement start-up, backing a technology that could lower future emissions across the economy.
tension: jobs now vs. innovation for the future

title: Reservoir Drawdown and the Buried Village
scenario: Dam operator Hanna Lindgren in Sweden can lower a reservoir to prevent downstream flooding after heavy rains. Lowering it quickly will expose the remains of a flooded village, including a cemetery, whose descendants hold annual remembrance ceremonies there, and the exposed mud may release stored pollutants. A slower drawdown protects both but risks flooding in a town downstream if rain continues. Weather forecasts are uncertain.
options: Lower the reservoir quickly, prioritising protection of the downstream town.
Lower it slowly, protecting the cemetery and avoiding pollutant release while accepting a risk of flooding.
Lower it moderately and stand ready to speed up if forecasts worsen, hoping the timing works out.
tension: safety of the living vs. respect for the dead
